unit.title: Age of Revolutions
unit.essential_question: How did ideas about the source of political power shift from the divine right of kings to the consent of the governed?
unit.footer: World History Hack™ — Unit 1: Age of Revolutions, Course Standard Edition.
unit.tn_connection: The Enlightenment ideas in this unit reached Tennessee directly. When the state wrote its first constitution in 1796, its Declaration of Rights opened by stating that “all power is inherent in the people, and all free governments are founded on their authority” — the same consent-of-the-governed principle John Locke argued (W.03) and the Declaration of Independence proclaimed in 1776 (W.08a). Thomas Jefferson praised Tennessee’s 1796 charter as “the least imperfect and most republican” of the state constitutions.
unit.tn_connection_task: The Enlightenment idea of consent of the governed shaped constitutions worldwide. Find one place in Tennessee's or the U.S. government where you can see 'consent of the governed' at work today, and record what you find.
unit.perspectives_intro: This unit's sourced record lets us weigh how monarchs, nobles, philosophers, and ordinary subjects each understood who should hold power — and why.
unit.belief_check: Before we begin: Where does a government's right to rule come from? Rank these from most to least legitimate — tradition, force, God, the people — and be ready to defend your order.
unit.play: Run a 'Two Thrones' debate: half the room argues as an absolute monarch's court, half as Enlightenment reformers, over one question — 'Who may limit the king?'
unit.spiral: These ideas (natural rights, social contract, consent of the governed) return in Unit 2 (French Revolution) and echo through every later revolution in the course.

W.01.title: Absolutism & the Divine Right of Kings

cfu.stem: Which statement best explains the idea of the divine right of kings?

options.A: A monarch's authority comes directly from God and cannot be questioned by subjects
options.B: A monarch's power is granted and limited by an elected assembly
options.C: A monarch must share power equally with the nobility
options.D: A monarch is chosen by a popular vote of the people

auth.close: By the late 1600s, several European rulers claimed absolute power — total authority over their lands, their laws, and their subjects. Many justified this with the divine right of kings: the belief that God had chosen the monarch, so resisting the king meant resisting God. In France, Louis XIV made himself the model of the absolute monarch. He built an enormous palace at Versailles and required leading nobles to live there, where lavish ceremonies kept them competing for his favor instead of challenging his rule. In Russia, Peter the Great held power just as tightly but used it differently: he forced a program of westernization, importing European technology, reorganizing the army, reducing the independence of the boyars, and building a new capital, St. Petersburg, as a 'window to the West.' Absolutism could unify a country and fund armies and monuments — but it concentrated so much on one person that a weak or reckless ruler could endanger the whole state.

cfu.stem: What key idea do BOTH the Magna Carta and the English Bill of Rights establish?

options.A: The monarch's power should be unlimited
options.B: The monarch is also bound by law and cannot rule without limits
options.C: The monarchy should be abolished entirely
options.D: Only the church may limit the king

auth.close: While Louis XIV was perfecting absolutism in France, England was moving the opposite direction. The change began long before, in 1215, when angry nobles forced King John to seal the Magna Carta. That charter established a revolutionary idea: even the king was under the law, and could not simply seize property or imprison free men without lawful judgment. Nearly five centuries later, after decades of conflict between monarchs and Parliament, the English Bill of Rights of 1689 went further. It gave Parliament control over taxes and armies, guaranteed free elections and free debate, and listed powers the monarch could not exercise alone. Together these documents built a constitutional monarchy — a state where a king or queen still reigned, but within limits set by law and Parliament. This was the sharpest contrast with the absolute monarchies of continental Europe, where rulers like Louis XIV recognized no such limits.

W.03.title: The Enlightenment: Reason, Rights & Government

auth.close: The Enlightenment was an explosion of confidence in human reason. Instead of accepting tradition or divine right, thinkers asked what reason alone could reveal about human nature and good government — and they disagreed sharply. Thomas Hobbes, writing in Leviathan after England's civil wars, believed people were selfish and life without strong authority would be 'nasty, brutish, and short'; he argued people trade freedom for a powerful ruler to keep order. John Locke disagreed. In his Second Treatise of Government he argued all people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and that government is a social contract to protect those rights — one the people may replace if it fails them. Baron de Montesquieu, in The Spirit of the Laws, proposed dividing power into separate branches so none could grow tyrannical. Jean-Jacques Rousseau, in The Social Contract, argued that legitimate government must follow the 'general will' of the people — popular sovereignty. These four blueprints would shape revolutions and constitutions for centuries.

cfu.stem: One major consequence of the English Civil War and the Glorious Revolution was that

options.A: England became an absolute monarchy like France
options.B: the divine right of kings was strengthened
options.D: the English monarch's power became limited by Parliament and law

auth.close: England's road to limited government ran through a brutal civil war. Kings James I and his son Charles I insisted on ruling by divine right and clashed with Parliament over taxes, religion, and power. When Charles I tried to govern without Parliament and then rule against it, war broke out in the 1640s between supporters of the king and supporters of Parliament. Parliament's forces, led by Oliver Cromwell, won — and in 1649 they did the unthinkable: they tried and executed Charles I, shattering the idea that a king was untouchable. Cromwell governed a republic called the Commonwealth, but after his death the monarchy was restored under Charles II. The struggle flared again under James II, until the nearly bloodless Glorious Revolution of 1688 replaced him with William and Mary — who accepted the English Bill of Rights and its limits on royal power. Out of decades of conflict, England had built a constitutional monarchy.

cfu.stem: The Declaration of Independence's phrase 'unalienable Rights... Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness' most directly reflects the ideas of

auth.close: The Enlightenment did not stay in Europe's salons — it crossed the Atlantic and helped spark a revolution. When Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence in 1776, he filled it with Enlightenment ideas, especially John Locke's. Locke had argued that all people have natural rights and that government exists by a social contract to protect them; Jefferson wrote that people are 'endowed... with certain unalienable Rights,' among them 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.' Locke had argued that a government failing its people may be replaced; Jefferson wrote that governments derive 'their just powers from the consent of the governed,' and that the people may alter or abolish a government that becomes destructive of those ends. Even the phrase 'self-evident' reflects the Enlightenment's faith that reason could reveal political truth. The Declaration shows how powerfully an idea — natural rights, consent of the governed — could move from a philosopher's page to the founding of a nation.
